newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Pressure mounts on S.Korean govt to save Kia.
newsitem.headline: Pressure mounts on S.Korean govt to save Kia.

text.p: The South Korean government on Wednesday faced mounting pressure on three fronts to keep the struggling Kia Group afloat, but analysts said any reprieve would be temporary.

The ruling New Korea Party accused the government of having a lukewarm attitude towards Kia and called for decisive action, while the militant Korean Confederation of Trade Unions vowed an all-out battle if authorities failed to act.
Finance Minister Kang Kyong-shik was scheduled to brief President Kim Young-sam on Kia's troubles on Wednesday afternoon, but there was no indication he would propose any intervention.
Adding to the tension, leading credit-rating agency Standard & Poor's Corp (S&P) announced it had placed five South Korean banks on Credit Watch with negative implications.
It said its action reflected an overall deterioration of asset quality in South Korea, as demonstrated by the Kia crisis, and heightened industry risks.
The five banks, which S&P said had a combined exposure to Kia of 1.7 trillion won ($1.9 billion), were Hanil Bank, Korea Exchange Bank, Korea First Bank, Korea Long-Term Credit Bank and Shinhan Bank.

A bank anti-bankruptcy committee put Kia under protection last week to keep the group from defaulting on debt payments. Kia had an estimated 9.54 trillion won in debts as at the end of May, while its debt-to-shareholder equity ratio was 523.6 percent as at the end of last year.
Kia ran into difficulty after a slump in domestic sales by its carmaking flagship Kia Motors Corp and heavy capital investment by its steelmaking unit Kia Steel.
Speaking on behalf of the New Korea Party, a policy maker said the government's "lukewarm attitude" towards Kia had to change.

"The government should not stand idly by any longer ... It has to assume responsibility and make an aggressive effort to solve Kia's problems," Kim Zoong-wie, chairman of the policy committee, told a party meeting.
He added the government should act to prevent the credibility of Korean companies and financial institutions from suffering in world markets.

The Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, representing 524,000 workers, vowed an all-out battle against the government "if it doesn't directly come forward with steps to normalise Kia and the automobile industry's operations".
"The government shouldn't sit back and rely on creditor banks to come up with rescue measures," a union statement said.
However, analysts said the government would sooner or later have to recognise that the group had no future.
"Kia is doomed. It's a dead white elephant," said Steve Marvin, head of research at Ssangyong Investment Securities.
"It's on a life support system for now, depleting national resources. Unless the government keeps it artificially alive, it has no chance of surviving on its own," he said.
Jon Chong-wha, an auto analyst at Hannuri-Salomon Securities said: "Why do public taxes have to be used in saving private companies?
"The government should come to its senses and let the group take its natural course into third-party receivership."
Separately, the Kia Group said it had raised an estimated 350 billion won in the past three days through cash discount sales of 47,766 vehicles.
Yoo Young-gul, president of Kia Motor Sales Corp, told reporters the cash would be used to settle sub-contractors' promissory notes and for emergency operations.
